Dad, what's a Sixpence? (JWP130)

This episode starts with my six-year-old walking up to me one afternoon and asking, "Dad, what's a sixpence?" I follow that question all the way down.

I dig into the 400-year life of the sixpence, a British coin quietly debased over decades until there was no silver left in it at all, and finally withdrawn in 1980, largely without anyone noticing while it happened. From there I get into what debasement actually looks like in real time, why every generation assumes the money it grows up with is permanent, and why being a good capital allocator means being a student of change as much as a student of markets.

Also covered: the books that have shaped how I think about money (Menger, Lynn Alden, Saifedean Ammous), where Bitcoin fits into this story without being the whole story, and the question I've been sitting with since that conversation: what do I own today that feels permanent, but probably isn't?

Just opened a PR hardening how Primal's web app encrypts keys at rest which is a bit meatier than the one I submitted this morning.

Previously the PIN encrypted an nsec with a single unsalted SHA-256 hash of the PIN and unauthenticated AES-CBC. The PR upgrades this to PBKDF2 (600k iterations, random salt) and AES-256-GCM, which makes brute-forcing a stored blob drastically more expensive and makes wrong PINs fail cleanly. Existing users are migrated automatically on their next unlock, so nobody has to re-enter anything.

It also encrypts the NIP-46 client transport key, which was previously plaintext in localStorage, using a non-extractable WebCrypto key.

At the end of my conventional software career, I do carry resentment.
https://cdn.nostrcheck.me/376d0f9f7602ab73d99a171c0cecfebae92b9e5a919e3ce9d52452b68008ea49.jpeg
Not because I was underpaid.

Because I was underused.

Too many years were spent pushing tickets, polishing dashboards, navigating corporate theatre, protecting weak decisions, and learning the politics of appearing useful.

Very little of it demanded the full force of my mind.

The industry speaks endlessly about innovation, but much of modern software work is obedience with better tooling.

Take the ticket.

Attend the meeting.

Repeat the approved opinion.

Do not challenge the architecture.

Do not threaten the hierarchy.

Do not build beyond the roadmap.

Linux taught me something different.

Linux taught me that the machine can be understood.

DamageBDD taught me that behaviour can be defined, verified, and held accountable.

ECAI taught me that the limits imposed by an industry are not necessarily the limits of computation.

So no, I do not look back and wish I had earned more.

I wish I had been given harder problems.

I wish I had pushed earlier.

I wish I had spent fewer years asking permission from people whose imagination ended at the next quarter.

The saddest waste in software is not failed code.

It is a powerful mind reduced to ticket throughput.

I am no longer building for approval.

I am building at the edge of what I can understand.

That is the only career track that remains.

Actually there is a lot of tolerance for unfair dice (on bouncy surfaces/good rolls). For a D6 with probabilities [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125, 0.03125] (extremely biased to one side), the effective entropy is still 75% of a Vegas quality die (1.937 bits vs 2.585 bits). So 99 dice rolls with a shitty die like this would still yield about 192 bits of entropy instead of 256, plenty of entropy.

How to calculate the entropy of a given die with given probabilities: https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/1162511_13f7274a73274112ad9a05f8d68f8f25.html

Simply test the probability distribution with a couple hundred rolls (on bouncy surfaces for good measure) get the fraction of each face that shows up, and do this calculation to find the entropy o'er roll of your die. Then make sure you do over 128 bits worth of rolling (good rolls), but 99 rolls covers all bases with most dice.

Cryptography is not a passing financial fashion. Elliptic curves already sit beneath digital signatures, secure communications, blockchains, identity systems and the machinery of computational trust.

They are part of the mathematical foundation of the modern world.

Yet another generation of young engineers is being trained to chase frameworks, prompts and platform abstractions without understanding the cryptographic primitives beneath them.

They are taught how to build applications on top of systems they cannot independently verify.

That is how a generation of talented young heroes gets blindsided: not through a lack of intelligence, but through leadership that confused institutional fashion with technical reality.

Crypto was never merely about coins.

It was always about who owns the keys, who verifies the claim, who controls the ledger and whether trust can survive without permission from an empire.

Ignore that foundation long enough, and the future will be built by the few who bothered to understand it.

Every pupil movement becomes a signal.

Interfaces become behavioural traps.
Education becomes compliance measurement.
Work becomes continuous neurological inspection.

What aroused you.
What held you.
What you tried not to see.

The final enclosure is not the body.

A society whose gaze is measured, predicted and redirected no longer possesses a public imagination.

The bleak future is not that the state will watch everyone.

It is that everyone will learn to watch themselves.

Eyes forward.
Attention obedient.
Deviation recorded.

Welcome to the panopticon state of being.

I am no longer asking whether the elliptic manifold exists.

I found it.

What is already engineering to the builder still appears to be speculation to the industry.

New components keep manifesting from the same underlying truth.

The system does not require a new philosophy every time it grows.
The invariants remain intact.
The geometry continues to hold.
The implementation keeps converging.

That is what real discovery feels like from the inside: not a sudden announcement, but an increasingly unavoidable structure.

To everyone else, it still looks like a mystery.

To me, it is already memory.

I am not chasing the next new thing.

I am standing at the edge of the fold where it is arriving.

Linux Taught Me How to Think
https://blossom.yakihonne.com/0deb763ee941947e4e300999236a53933a33220325e75f155cf51885e5e2c3ea.jpeg
The best way to learn how to think in the modern age may not be another course in abstract reasoning.

It may simply be to use Linux.

As an undergraduate, Linux first feels like unnecessary difficulty. You only want the machine to do one small thing, but suddenly you are reading documentation, fixing permissions, inspecting logs and discovering that three different configuration files can all influence the same result.

Nothing is hidden behind a friendly “Something went wrong” message.

The system gives you evidence.

At first, you copy commands from forums. Then one of those commands breaks something, and you learn the first real lesson: never execute what you do not understand.

Slowly, the terminal stops looking like a wall of text. You begin to see processes, pipes, files, users, signals, sockets and dependencies. A computer is no longer a mysterious appliance. It becomes a collection of understandable parts interacting under explicit rules.

That changes how you approach problems.

You stop asking:

> “Which button fixes this?”



You start asking:

> “What state is the system in, what changed, and where is the evidence?”



By the time you become a professional, Linux has quietly trained several habits into you:

Read the error. Inspect the environment. Reduce the problem. Test one assumption at a time. Automate what repeats. Keep recovery paths. Understand the layer beneath your abstraction.

It also teaches humility. The machine does not care about your title, confidence or deadline. A misplaced character is still a misplaced character. Reality refuses to negotiate.

Over time, Linux becomes more than an operating system. It becomes a workshop for thought.

You enter as a student trying to make the computer obey.

You leave as an engineer who has learned to observe systems, question assumptions and reason from evidence.

Mathematics teaches formal thought.

Linux teaches what happens when formal thought meets a living machine.
